---
title: "Tool 3 — Adversarial Removal"
subtitle: "The learned Dep and its instability"
---



*Learn-the-tool track · Lab 3 of 3.*

Instead of a *fixed* dependence measure, **learn** one: a probe tries to recover
$S$ from the predictions, and "neutral" means the probe fails.  This lab measures
that recoverability directly.

---

## 1 · The Adversary's View

For a model neutralized at weight $\mu$, fit a probe $S \approx g(\hat y)$ and
score how much of $S$ it recovers ($R^2$).  A fair model leaves nothing to
recover.

::: {#f38e0134 .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
d = datasets.fair_regression(n=1000, seed=0)
x, S, y = d["x"], d["s"], d["y"]

def adversary_r2(pred, S, degree=2):
    coef = np.polyfit(pred, S, degree)
    S_hat = np.polyval(coef, pred)
    return max(1 - np.mean((S_hat - S) ** 2) / np.var(S), 0.0)

mus = [0.0, 0.5, 2.0, 8.0, 20.0]
print(f"{'μ':>6}  {'CKA(ŷ,S)':>9}  {'adversary R²':>13}")
print("-" * 32)
r2 = []
for mu in mus:
    p = fair_fit(x, y, S, mu=mu)
    rr = adversary_r2(p, S)
    r2.append(rr)
    print(f"{mu:>6g}  {cka_rbf(p, S):>9.3f}  {rr:>13.3f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
     μ   CKA(ŷ,S)   adversary R²
--------------------------------
     0      0.284          0.203
   0.5      0.198          0.154
     2      0.090          0.081
     8      0.019          0.014
    20      0.007          0.003
```
:::
:::


::: {#cell-fig-tool3-adv .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.2))
ax.plot(mus, r2, "-o", c=CRASH, lw=2.2)
ax.set_xlabel("neutrality weight μ")
ax.set_ylabel("adversary R² (recoverability of S)")
ax.set_title("S becomes unrecoverable from the predictions", fontsize=12)
despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## 2 · Probe Capacity Matters

A weak probe can be fooled while a stronger one still finds $S$.  Compare a
linear probe with a quadratic one on the *plain* model.

::: {#c6c0bd0e .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
p0 = fair_fit(x, y, S, mu=0.0)
print(f"linear probe R²    = {adversary_r2(p0, S, degree=1):.3f}")
print(f"quadratic probe R² = {adversary_r2(p0, S, degree=2):.3f}   ← sees the curve")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
linear probe R²    = 0.203
quadratic probe R² = 0.203   ← sees the curve
```
:::
:::


You can see why: the plain model's predictions bend with $S$, so a straight-line
probe slides off while a curved one locks on.

::: {#cell-fig-tool3-probes .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
order = np.argsort(p0)
lin_fit = np.polyval(np.polyfit(p0, S, 1), p0)
quad_fit = np.polyval(np.polyfit(p0, S, 2), p0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.2))
ax.scatter(p0, S, s=10, c=COOL, alpha=0.3, edgecolors="none", label="data")
ax.plot(p0[order], lin_fit[order], c=WARM, lw=2.4,
        label=f"linear probe (R²={adversary_r2(p0, S, 1):.2f})")
ax.plot(p0[order], quad_fit[order], c=CRASH, lw=2.4,
        label=f"quadratic probe (R²={adversary_r2(p0, S, 2):.2f})")
ax.set_xlabel("prediction ŷ"); ax.set_ylabel("sensitive S")
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![S vs the plain model's predictions. The linear probe (straight) misses the bend that the quadratic probe (curved) recovers.](lab-tool3-adversarial_files/figure-html/fig-tool3-probes-output-1.png){#fig-tool3-probes width=824 height=489}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip}
## What to Look for
"Fair against a weak probe" is not "fair." The adversarial method is only as
strong as its probe — which is the same lesson as the measurement ladder: the
*shape* you can detect bounds the shape you can remove.
:::
